#4250. Marvel Cosmic Invasion's Doctor Doom-Themed DLC Gives It The Post-Game Tail It Was Missing

Marvel Cosmic Invasion was a bit of a dream game for me; I loved the X-Men arcade game in the '90s, so when Tribute Games released the excellent Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles: Shredder's Revenge in 2022, I immediately hoped they'd revitalize other licensed brawler franchises released by Konami in the late '80s and early '90s. While we still haven't heard any word of a new brawler starring The Simpsons, Tribute did follow up its Turtle triumph with Marvel Cosmic Invasion, another throwback side-scrolling beat 'em up, this time starring Marvel's mightiest.

I played through Marvel Cosmic Invasion multiple times and had a blast, but I moved on quickly, as I didn't feel the need to collect different palette-swaps of the many heroes on offer. Even after Cyclops and The Thing joined the roster as DLC in May, I still saw Cosmic Invasion as a game in the rearview. That changes this week, as The Siege of Castle Doom not only adds two additional playable characters (Invisible Woman and Doctor Doom), but also a mode that has the potential to bring me back for more runs for the foreseeable future.

Seeing that Annihilus is threatening the universe, Doom decides to take matters into his own hands. Unfortunately, much in the way that it seems that he may try to fix the multiversal incursions in the upcoming Avengers: Doomsday, Victor Von Doom's solution in Marvel Cosmic Invasion – the Cosmic Inductor – would lead to untold death and destruction. In The Siege of Castle Doom, you select your team and fight your way through various floors of the stronghold belonging to the man who is perhaps Marvel's greatest villain. Your goal is to fight through the winding, randomized hallways of Castle Doomstadt, charging Reed Richards' Stabilizer and tactically bolstering your team along the way, before Doctor Doom can enact his plan.

As for the new playable characters, Doctor Doom is less agile, but his attacks pack a whallop, while Invisible Woman's force fields and speed make her the more versatile pick. I don't know that I see either of them replacing my mains from the base game, but I had fun experimenting with them throughout this mode. Regardless of which character you choose from the expanding roster, you still must traverse Castle Doomstadt before Doom achieves his objective.

Fighting through waves of enemies across differently themed and booby-trapped rooms, you encounter all manner of foes from the base game, as well as new minion types from Doom. When you defeat enemies, they drop batteries that charge your Stabilizer, letting you even the odds and stop Doom. Conversely, each time an enemy hits your character, it charges Doom's Cosmic Inductor, inching him closer to victory and making his minions faster and stronger in the process. As you might expect, the rooms get harder the deeper you go, and while each player starts with two characters to swap between, if a character completely depletes their health, they're gone for good, making it even tougher. As such, you need to keep your eyes on each character's health and swap them out when it makes sense.

As you complete each room, you can choose which path to take to augment your characters with new special abilities. True to the roguelite structure, as you complete rooms, you can also buff your characters' stats within the run. Certain rooms offer extra batteries to help your Stabilizer charge, while others offer new and upgraded equipment. There's also one that promises random events that can easily alter the trajectory of your run for better or worse. Though I often enjoyed boosting attack stats to make enemies less like damage sponges, I had to balance that against buffing their health to keep them alive and charging the Stabilizer to have a fighting chance.

Beyond the in-run upgrades and modifiers, you can also amp up the action run-over-run through upgrades in Reed's Lab, which add to the pool of modifiers you can select from at the start of each run. The expansion also adds new palettes for existing heroes, plus new music by composer Tee Lopes. While I've only done a few runs of The Siege of Castle Doom (each taking between 45 and 90 minutes, depending on how successful you are), I feel a revitalized sense of excitement for Marvel Cosmic Invasion. Tribute claims completionists can spend upwards of 15 hours in this new mode, which has me champing at the bit to dive back into what will likely be my primary way of interacting with Marvel Cosmic Invasion going forward.

Marvel Cosmic Invasion – The Siege of Castle Doom is available today on all platforms, and it is a strong addition to an already great game. You can read our review of the base version of Marvel Cosmic Invasion here.

#4248. Nioh 3’s generous demo is out now, and your progress carries over to the full game

If you’re looking for a way to check out one of the biggest releases of early 2026, Team Ninja has made it easy for you.

Nioh 3 is one of the most anticipated games of 2026, and it’s easily among the biggest releases of February. We’re a few days away from the start of that month, however, but we don’t have to wait until then to actually play Team Ninja’s next major release.

The previously announced demo has arrived, and it’s one any fan of action games should check out, especially if you missed the PlayStation-exclusive beta held last year.

Unlike previous tests, the Nioh 3 demo is available on PC and PS5, just like the main game. This is pretty new for the series, which has typically launched first on PlayStation before coming to PC months later.

The Nioh 3 demo includes a decent portion of content from the beginning of the game. It’s enough to show off the core duality mechanic, letting you switch between the Samurai and Ninja styles at will. It also includes a preview of the game’s open field level design, which makes it sit somewhere between full open world and the more linear level design of past Nioh games.

Feedback from the previous beta has been implemented into the demo (and full release), so you may see some familiar faces, as well as areas you visited before - assuming you played that one.

Another big reason why you might want to grab the Nioh 3 demo is that your progress in it will carry over to the full version. This includes the character creator, too, meaning you can spend all day perfecting your character without having to worry about missing out on playing the actual game.

The demo even supports online multiplayer for up to three players, in case you come to Nioh for co-op. If you complete the available content, you’ll earn an in-game bonus in the full version. This is something Team Ninja has done with past Nioh titles, of course.

This time, your reward is the Twin-Snake Helmet. Just make sure you complete the demo before February 15.

Nioh 3 is out February 6 on PC, and PlayStation 5.

#4247. Marathon’s Symbiosis Update Adds Host Of New Modes, Including Permanent PvE, Next Month

Bungie has detailed its upcoming Symbiosis update for Marathon, which introduces several significant modes next month. Chief among them is the new permanent PvE mode, which Bungie previously experimented with and promised earlier this year.

Symbiosis is headlined by Expedition, a co-op PvE destination with roguelite elements. Expedition pits teams of players against escalating challenges and offers randomized upgrades called Flash Boosts to increase their odds of success.

The Perimeter zone has also been expanded with the new Burrows and Reservoir areas. Another addition is Limbo, a new social hub for players to gather that features a firing range. You can also try out the new sword-wielding Bishop Runner Shell alongside new weapons and gear, such as the Maverick pistol, throwing knife, hack grenade, and V17 flamethrower. Lastly, you can test your skills against other players in the beta PvP Deathmatch mode.

Symbiosis arrives in Marathon on December 8. An open play week will kick off the same day, allowing new players to experience all of Marathon’s content for free until December 15.

The Symbiosis update marks Marathon's evolution into a more co-op-friendly, PvE experience as its initial focus on PvP extraction has struggled to sustain a substantial audience since its March 5 launch. Bungie announced in September that it plans to spend the rest of 2026 improving Marathon's core mechanics and features while giving players more agency for how they engage with it beyond competitive PvP.

#4246. Postal Classic & Uncut is a rough port of a PC classic, and shows how different gaming is today

With the launch of Grand Theft Auto VI this week, the conversation has inevitably turned to the content and how controversial it is. Small wonder then that one of the most unusual launches for Android has gone overlooked as a result. But what Postal Classic & Uncut represents as it hits Google Play is a massive shift in how we view violence in gaming, as mere decades ago it would have been unthinkable to have something like this available on mobile.

Now, admittedly, Postal isn’t a total stranger to mobile. But the top-down shooter by the same name we had all the way back in 2010 is undoubtedly a very different animal from today’s Postal series, or even the 1997 original. So, what’s changed? And why hasn’t this once-controversial shooter seen the same attention now it’s out on Google Play? Going Postal It’s a sign of the times that I need to explain what made Postal so controversial. Aside from being able to recklessly murder civilians in graphic (for the time) fashion, you would also be running and gunning through recognisable recreations of real-world locations, rather than more abstract futuristic bases and winding dungeons of games like Doom and Quake.

In Postal, you play as the Postal Dude, a deranged maniac convinced the entire world is out to get him. Through rambling diary entries and interludes, we get a peek into his deteriorating mental state as he moves from level to level, gunning down the cops and armed responders trying to stop him with bullets, grenades and petrol bombs. All while innocent civilians are caught up in the crossfire.

Postal, essentially, was the first major shooter to offer you the ability to wantonly murder people who weren’t a threat to you. And being set in a recognisable, albeit stylised version of America, coming at a time when mass shootings were becoming more and more of a problem, it’s not hard to see why Postal courted controversy with press and politicians alike for being a murder simulator.

One notable sequence sees you firebombing a marching band, a scene that’s equal parts ludicrous and grisly. Even the name itself prompted a reaction from the USPS, which sued over the association of the name with the term ‘going postal’ that had become popularised after several high-profile shootings by United States Postal Workers.

Postal on mobile I’d originally intended to build this whole op-ed around a review of Postal Classic & Uncut. In truth, it can be summed up as ‘boy, this has aged poorly’. And not in the Postal II way, where the crass political and social satire has lost any edge and just become distasteful, but because it’s simply not very good. Or at the very least this mobile port certainly isn’t.

The controls are awkward, the graphics are so condensed as to be unrecognisable, and even the run ‘n gun gameplay suffers from a poor auto-aim system that makes using any weapon other than your starting infinite-ammo SMG impractical at best. All that, plus the repetitive dialogue from enemies as you gun them down, makes you feel irritation more than sadistic amusement or horror and revulsion.

It got me thinking about how massively controversial Postal had once been, how its gruesome and ‘realistic’ violence had been seen as a harbinger of moral decay. Meanwhile, decades later, the most violent game series most people know is now a vehicle for doing chores and buying groceries. And Postal itself is now available on the same storefront as Candy Crush.

It’s hard not to see the irony in the fact that violence is no longer as shocking in gaming as it once was, to the point that it’s being actively sidelined in favour of character interaction and random menial tasks.

But I think this represents a very strange and interesting moment in gaming. Now, a series condemned for its violence is forcing players to do something unthinkable and get a (digital) life. Meanwhile, Postal’s vicarious depictions of murder and mayhem don’t even seem quaint anymore, but actively cringeworthy in how blatantly edgy they feel.

Even Postal Redux, which remastered the original shooter, chose to revamp the run ‘n gun gameplay, adding in a pulse-pounding soundtrack and seemingly dialling up the mayhem to make it more an action romp than a chilling thriller. I think I was expecting something like the experience I had playing Redux when I stepped into Postal Classic & Uncut, but instead it was just a bit boring.

That’s not to say I think Postal Classic & Uncut is entirely worthless in execution. Its grim, unrelenting strangeness and lack of a soundtrack, with just the eerie sounds of the wind and gunshots, make it thoroughly unnerving to play. Add the Son of Sam-style diary interludes, and you get a very disturbing glimpse into a mind that’s on the verge of slipping completely. ‘Gone’ Postal Bottom line, it feels as though the days of graphic violence have really run their course as a storytelling device. Postal Classic & Uncut then functions more as a snapshot of the 90s, a moment in time that shows us when the very idea of seeing someone pull a trigger and a random innocent fall down was considered so shocking and controversial that it needed condemnation.

But the fact is that the Postal Dude was only ever explored at a surface level, and his fragile psychological state was never the focus. There’s an irony there that the act, and not the motivation, is what shocks us so much. Even Running With Scissors are attempting to switch gears, not focusing on the mayhem but the emotional impact, with games such as the upcoming Flesh & Wire recasting the protagonist as the survivor of one of the Dude’s rampages; perhaps even the one shown in the original Postal.

It’s a telling lesson that you can show people the most gruesome, unbelievable things imaginable. Ultimately though, to them it’s just images on a screen, and only by establishing the context and people around them does it become something truly grisly. Does that mean violence is passe? Will the next Postal feature the dude having a nice Sunday walk, no guns or satire included?

Obviously, the answer to that question, and a way to truly shock and offend the right-minded people of the world, is for Running With Scissors to re-release Postal Babes.

#4244. 10 Best Easter Eggs in GTA 6

Aden Carter is a Contributor at DualShockers who has been covering games professionally since 2020. He specializes in lists and guides, with a focus on RPGs, horror games, survival horror, Soulslikes, cozy/sim games, and action-adventure titles. Before joining DualShockers, Aden contributed to GameRant, XDA, Gamepur, I

The most common thing for any game developer to do is to make nods to different franchises in their game. Affectionately called easter eggs, these little details are meant to be surprises for players who love various other franchises.

Whether you are a fan of games, television shows, or movies, there’s plenty to discover in Grand Theft Auto 6. Rockstar has taken the time to hide trophies all around Leonida for those who are diligent enough to go searching for them. Even 'Weird Al' Yankovic is hiding in this game somewhere.

Have you found Dexter’s apartment? Maybe you have gone searching for the literal easter egg. Either way, these are amazing nods to other franchises in the mighty GTA 6.

Dexter is a very popular television series about a vigilante serial killer. This serial killer just so happens to live in Miami, which just so happens to be the city that Vice City is based on. What a coincidence!

It just so happens that Rockstar noticed this connection and decided to add a few nods to the series in GTA 6, with the first of them being Dexter’s apartment, which is located on Washington Island.

Of course, you won’t be able to reach this area right away, but once you get access to the map, you can head straight there to check it out and pay tribute to the television series. You can also find some tools on the roof.

Bigfoot has decided to make his way out of the northern forests and headed south to the marshlands of Leonida. It’s a bit weird that he decided to make this island paradise his home, but I won’t question that.

If you progress through the story of GTA 6, there is a mission that will set you on the path to discovering Bigfoot, but he is easy to overlook, as he runs away rather quickly once you get near him.

I barely caught a glimpse of him, but chased him down and caught a photo before he mysteriously disappeared into the marsh. I have no idea if I will see him again, but it was cool to catch a glimpse of this mysterious figure.

After Grand Theft Auto 5's release, the Mount Chiliad mystery was one of the most talked about easter eggs out there. Here's what we know today.

Some developers make nods to different games or pop culture, but Rockstar takes the time to put a literal easter egg in its game. That’s right, if you go to the correct spot on the map, you can find a nest with literal easter eggs in it.

The location in question is a radio tower in South Vice Dale County. The radio tower takes multiple minutes to climb, but the payoff is definitely worth it, as you find a nest full of easter eggs at the top.

While I won’t spoil what happens when you throw one, it does involve a cutscene, and you should definitely take the time to visit the location and watch it unfold.

One of the most memorable missions in GTA 5 is when Michael’s boat gets stolen and you need to chase down the people responsible. Unfortunately, Michael’s boat doesn’t get returned, but we now know the whereabouts of it, and it turns out that it landed in Jason’s yard.

Next to Jason’s house, there is a run-down boat that looks similar to Michael’s. People have pointed this out for a while, but there was no confirmation until now.

Since the game is officially out, you can check out the boat, and you can even climb on top of it. Once there, you can use your phone’s camera to check out the display. Doing so will allow you to see a display that shows part of the GTA 5 map, seemingly confirming that this is Michael’s boat.

Have you ever heard of a movie called Island Claws? If not, you aren’t the only one, but there is a nod to this film in GTA 6. The movie is from the 1980s, and it is about a scientist who genetically modifies crabs to make them grow larger to solve world hunger.

Unfortunately, this doesn’t work out very well, and a similar thing has transpired in Leonida. In Pelican Valley, you can find a trail of blood that leads to a shack. Inside the shack, you can find information about failed experiments on crabs.

Along with this, Jason will get attacked by a giant crab that jumps down on him from the ceiling. It is a rather large easter egg that is meant to pay homage to the classic independent film. Good job doing your research Rockstar.

One of the things that people loved to do in Grand Theft Auto 5 was break into the military base, and the go-to means of breaking into the base was via the hill jump just outside the fence along the highway.

Well, there is another military base in GTA 6 and it is located near where you start the game. It is called Mile Zero Air Station, and it has a convenient hill just outside the fence that you can use to jump into the base just like in GTA 5.

There is no way that this is a coincidence because the hill is an obvious jumping point. Thank you Rockstar for including an obvious homage to the previous game and the silly antics players got into.

From drawings in a mental hospital to TV and radio commercials, these are nine Rockstar Games Easter Eggs that hint at a shared universe.

The most common meme that has ever been spread about a video game is probably the, “We got [insert item here] before GTA 6.” It popped up every single time something major happened before the release of the game. Well it can’t be said anymore since the game is out.

With that being said, the meme will probably become about either Elder Scrolls 6 or GTA 7, or maybe even RAC 7. You might be wondering what that is. Well, if you scroll through your phone’s Snapmatic app, you can find a post about a game called Barnyard Blue: Hot Pursuit.

The post reads, “Barnyard Blue video game before Race and Chase 7 is crazy.” There is even a comment that reads, “We really got Barnyard Blue games before RAC 7.” This is, of course, a jab at the classic meme that appeared for so many years.

The X-Men actually exist in the Grand Theft Auto universe, except they don’t exist in the same way as you know them. Instead of being called the X-Men, they are referred to as the RX-Men. A strange choice, but one that makes it obvious that it is a reference to the classic hero team.

There are various magazines that you can find in the different convenience stores around Leonida, but you can reliably find this magazine in the 24-7 supermarket in northern Key Lento.

In this story, you can find a copy of RX-Men issue 13 titled, “Paging Dr. Placebo.” It features GTA renditions of different heroes and villains. There’s also collectible cards for these characters sprinkled around Leonida.

Speaking of trading cards, you can find various wrestling trading cards across Leonida. This is an obvious easter egg to the various wrestling trading cards that already exist. The wrestling company is called B.A.M, and it stands for Backyard American Mania.

Florida has a rather large wrestling scene, with the WWE training facility being in Orlando. On top of this, various famous wrestlers live or lived in Florida.

To go even further, the acronym of B.A.M. can also be related to Bird Azarian Memorial Training Center, which is located in Illinois, but is a wrestling training center. Odds are, it is just a reference to WWE wrestling.

Early in the game, Jason and Cal sit down to play some games on the JoyStation, with the system itself being an obvious reference to the PlayStation 5. However, that isn’t the whole easter egg, as the game that is played is called Tenebrae Lux.

Tenebrae Lux is a game themed after the movie called The Lighthouse, which features both Robert Pattinson and Willem Dafoe. This is awesome, but there is yet one more easter egg hidden here.

The name Tenebrae Lux is Latin for the term “light-dark.” This happens to be the exact translation of the French term Clair Obscur, which is one of the greatest games to have been released in recent years and a game that took the world by storm.

This list delves into some of the best Easter eggs in video games, exploring how to unlock them, what they're referencing, and more.

#4242. Surprising Literally Nobody, Grand Theft Auto VI Is The Most Pre-Ordered Game In PlayStation And Xbox Store History

Grand Theft Auto VI launches next week on Thursday, November 19. You can preload the game on PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X/S starting today, as detailed by Rockstar Games, PlayStation, and Xbox. Alongside this announcement, both PlayStation and Xbox have revealed that – surprise! – GTA VI is the most preordered game in the history of their respective digital stores.

That's not shocking – GTA VI is, by many metrics, the most anticipated game in history, with its predecessor, Grand Theft Auto V, selling nearly 235 million copies since its launch back in 2013. There's also the fact that Rockstar Games is not releasing a physical edition of GTA VI, per se. Yes, you can go to a store to pick up a GTA VI box (and you can do so today, allowing you to preload the game), but inside that box will be a download code for a digital version of the game – you won't find GTA VI on a physical disc. So, naturally, many players are opting to purchase the game on digital storefronts like the PlayStation and Xbox game stores.

"Grand Theft Auto VI, the most preordered title of all time on the Microsoft Store, launches November 19," an Xbox blog post reads. "Considering the unprecedented demand, we encourage everyone to begin preloading as soon as possible to ensure you're prepared for launch day." PlayStation echoes this statement with a blog post of its own that reads, "Grand Theft Auto VI is now the most preordered game in the history of the PlayStation Store. Given this unprecedented demand, we've joined with Rockstar Games to allow players to start preloading the game nine days early, so they're ready to play on launch day."

There you have it: People are very excited about Grand Theft Auto VI.

Grand Theft Auto VI launches next week on November 19 on PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X/S.

For more, check out the song "Pusher" from the game's original score, then check out the GTA VI launch trailer. After that, check out this exclusive story about how GTA VI features over 170 animal species and another about its tropical storms and hurricanes. Be sure to read about how GTA VI will target 30 FPS gameplay on all consoles, too.

#4241. Infinity Nikki ushers in the Year of the Horse with... a deer-themed Version 2.2

Chromatic Beings Everbright, the latest major Infinity Nikki update, has arrived, bringing Chinese New Year celebrations vibe to the game.

Infinity Nikki, the free-to-play, open-world dress-up RPG, has delivered yet another big content drop in the form of Chromatic Beings Everbright. The latest update brings the game up to version 2.2, and introduces a new narrative chapter, and gameplay taking place around a festival narrative.

If you couldn’t guess already, the new theme is Bloom Festival, inspired by Chinese New Year celebrations.

The big new story chapter takes place in the Infinity Nikki’s Wanxiang Realm. This deceptively serene and blissful region hides a dark secret, however. Chromafaces, the mythical inhabitants of the realm, have to embody fixed identities that dictate how they live and work.

These are doled out through Character Tokens, which are used to assign roles to each individual. The story follows Nikki as she uncovers the script that runs the realm and the facade it props up. Nikki will help free Chromafaces and dispel the illusion.

The Wanxiang Realm is split into three areas. Cai Ye is your typical lantern-lit district, where festivals and fireworks happen. Kongming Gorge is almost the opposite of that; a quiet and cold place. Finally, Jiuhua Pavilion literally floats above the region, and it's home to neverending music and dance.

The other big addition in 2.2 are the two new 5-Star Resonance Outfits with some interesting gameplay implications. Where Wanxiang Weaves Life is inspired by wuxia aesthetics, and true to its inspirations, it lets Nikki shapeshift into different Spirit Personas - and automatically collect resources in her vicinity.

Chroma's Mortal Heart, on the other hand, allows Nikki to fly around the Wanxiang Realm, drawing on the power of the Celestial Deer. This outfit also uses Celestial Deer Vision to automatically ping and mark treasure chests around her.

You can also look forward to Nefarious Shadows, a new Ability Outfit, which lets Nikki see through disguises, and reveals hidden paths in the world.

As with every major update, of course, there are themed activities and limited-time events throughout. Hotpot House is a cooking minigame where you attempt to run the eponymous restaurant, whereas Flavor Frenzy is series of platforming challenges that tasks you with gathering ingredients. Fortune Mahjong is a little more straightforward, with support for solo and multiplayer play.

If you’re jumping back into the game soon, be sure to hit up our Infinity Nikki codes page for some freebies.

#4238. GTA 6: Best Starter Car to Register

Christian Bognar is a Contributor at DualShockers with over three years of experience covering the gaming industry. Since 2022, he has written guides and reviews for publications including DualShockers, CBR, Attack of the Fanboy, PC Invasion, and The Game Slayer. He holds a Bachelor’s Degree in Business Administration

During your Grand Theft Auto 6 playthrough, you will eventually get the opportunity to register a car. Registering cars allows you to call them easily from your phone with a small BuckMe fee.

This opportunity comes at the start of Chapter 2, where you learn about a man named Moses who deals with stolen cars. To unlock Moses and his shop for good, you need to bring him your very first car to register.

Instead of stealing the coolest car to register, I recommend going a different route. Here’s the best starter car to register in GTA 6.

During the first mission of Chapter 2 in GTA 6, you will naturally meet a girl named Vicki. During this mission, Vicki will eventually mention Moses to Lucia, and once she does, Moses shop will be marked on the map with the objective to bring him a starter car to register.

Find the red Phoenix in GTA 6’s Unwanted Attention mission, sneak through the police impound, escape the cops, and deliver the car to Brian.

After bringing Moses one car and registering it with him for free, you will unlock the ability to register most cars in Leonida. The only cars you can’t register with Moses are the ones with trackers, so make a mental note of that.

Also, keep in mind that even though you can register your starter car for free, registering every other car from here on out will cost you money. The price of registration depends on the type of car.

While players may want to steal and register the flashiest car in Leonida as their starter, this isn’t necessarily the smartest move. The nice sports cars won’t have the most trunk space and can be hard to control.

Instead, it would be best to choose a pickup truck for a starter car, as they have a ton of stash space and are generally easy to drive.

Find GTA 6 Ultimate Edition vehicles, weapons, clothing, and hairstyles, and learn which chapters and locations unlock each item.

It may seem unimportant, but having more stash space will allow Lucia to transport more money and robbery loot on a single trip. This means you can gather money faster, without constantly needing to visit ATMs.

Additionally, as previously mentioned, pickup trucks are generally on the easier side to control when driving. This is important early in the game since it will allow you to have an easier time exploring, crashing less, and avoiding the need to pay for repairs.

Once you've built up wealth by using your starter car as a getaway and stash for loot from robberies and muggings, you can use any extra cash to register nicer vehicles.

Simply put, the coolest cars tend to have the highest registration price, so you want a reliable one that will help you get around easier and stash more money to start off.

Find a tank at Mile Zero Air Station in GTA 6. Learn where to enter the base, where the tanks are parked, and what to expect when you escape.

While there are many pickup trucks to find across the map of GTA VI, I have had the best luck finding them in parking lots. More specifically, I have found pickup trucks commonly in parking lots in front of bars, clothing shops, barbershops, etc.

In other words, pickup trucks are very easy to find, considering they aren’t that special when it comes to style and speed and aren’t considered “rare.” If you are worried about finding one in a specific color, you shouldn’t be, considering Moses makes you change the color when you bring it in.

Once you find a pickup truck (or a different car if you decided not to listen to my advice), bring it on over to Moses and tell him you’d like to register it.

After the quick transaction with Moses is complete, you are now able to call your starter car to your location whenever you like for a small BuckMe price via the Scooter Bros app on your phone.

#4237. Australia Did It: End-of-the-World Railway Defense Business Review - Delivering Where It Matters

Australia Did It: End-of-the-world Railway Defense Business is a game I catch myself playing in my head long after I shut it off. Though it uses turn-based strategy as its base, it expands beyond the genre’s regular confines, blending elements from roguelikes, puzzle games, bullet-heaven titles, and the tower-defense genre. The result is an experience that demands wide-scale experimentation and rewards improvisation.

In a post-apocalyptic world where the Atlantic Ocean has dried up, you risk your life to ensure your shipment reaches its destination. Riding from station to station by train, you must build your team amid your many missions as various mutated creatures, malicious machines, and coordinated soldiers attack your convoy. Lore is doled out piecemeal and serves mostly as background dressing, but each time I learned more about the world, I became more curious.

To survive the harshness of the wasteland, you must use cindermint, an in-game resource gained for surviving turns and killing enemies, to spawn defenders, with three base classes to choose from. The revolver-wielding Gunslinger is your primary damage dealer, while the Radshot applies corrosive radiation damage, and the Nomad offers a close-range shotgun blast with knockback.

Those base-level characters offer solid variety upon which to build. And that’s where the main hook for Australia Did It comes in: experimentation through combination. In the midst of battle, you can merge two units of the same level to create new, more powerful defenders, influenced by the traits of those used in the merge. At the onset, you can merge two Nomads to create a level 2 Nomad with increased damage and knockback, but the real fun comes in combining disparate units to create completely new characters. Even now, more than 15 hours into my gameplay, I’m still concocting new combinations I want to try on my next run.

By the end of my first successful run, I had multiple level 6 characters, including a railgun-toting heavy, mages who steal health from enemies and redistribute it to nearby allies, a drone that can move beyond the walls of the station to attack enemies directly, and, my personal favorite, a dual-shotgun-wielding one-man wrecking crew. However, many of these higher-level units also possess drawbacks to consider, like the railgun scorching all adjacent tiles or the drone running out of battery if it’s outside the walls for too long. Though I started keeping notes in my head about which combinations led to my favorite results, I was grateful for a comprehensive compendium that tracked the tens of unit types I unlocked through this rewarding experimentation.

The meat of the experience places your squad on a 25-tile square board with enemies spawning from the four principal directions. Thoughtfulness and positioning are crucial, as each unit on your squad possesses different traits and movement efficiency, as do the encroaching enemies. Basic enemies often make a beeline toward the station, while others may take a weaving route or keep their distance and blast you at range. Improvising and adjusting your strategy on the fly is the most engaging part of Australia Did It, and when you perfectly adapt in the moment, or escape the scenario by the skin of your teeth, there are few better feelings I’ve experienced in a game this year.

Your goal in this phase is to simply defend the station and gather resources to strengthen your squad before evacuating and moving on to the next area. Considering each unit's strengths, weaknesses, and capabilities while strategically positioning them around the station takes some getting used to, especially during the more chaotic stages. I fist-pumped as I watched the train pull out of a station that was about to crumble, and I lamented the loss of high-level units I had to leave behind to ensure the survival of the convoy. The process is ceaselessly thrilling, even as you begin to see how the gears work under the hood. I just wish I could say the same about the intervening train sections.

Once you escape the turn-based strategy portion, your surviving squad members hop aboard the train and chart their route. Using a basic map, you choose your next stop, with factors like enemy types and modifiers shown to you ahead of time. The top-down train segments between station-defense stages are largely passive; the units you evacuated from the previous station automatically attack swarming enemies with the same traits and perks they have in the main gameplay areas. You can aim a focus cone to instruct your units, but you’re at the mercy of the units you’ve brought. You can trigger an ultimate ability to send your defenders into overdrive, but I rarely needed it.

While I love the idea of intentionally crafting a team that’s good at both the turn-based strategy and bullet-heaven transport sections, I was never fully engaged getting from point A to point B. Instead, I often caught myself checking how much longer before my train arrived at the next station; these sections can be completed in a minute or two, but that doesn’t alleviate the feeling that it’s a step down from the other gameplay. These novel portions aren’t bad by any means; they’re merely an average part of an otherwise excellent experience.

Looking back on the hours I poured into Australia Did It, the forgettable train segments will occupy only a small part of my memories, just as they do in each run. Instead, what will stick with me for months to come are the creative combination mechanics, the outstanding turn-based defense system, and the thrill of uncovering the mysteries of this bleak, yet engaging world.

#4236. Zenelss Zone Zero Version 2.6 has you playing as an event planner and social media manager for an idol group

Zenelss Zone Zero's Encore for an Old Dream has a good excuse for introducing some new mechanics to the action game.

Zenless Zone Zero’s latest Special Program has delivered a tonne of information about the game’s big upcoming update, Version 2.6. This latest addition kicks off celebrations in New Eridu, and it’s dubbed Encore for an Old Dream.

Version 2.6 is not far off, either, arriving in ZZZ on February 6 - exactly one week from today. Encore for an Old Dream is something of an in-between story that takes place after the end of Season 2.

The narrative of 2.6 sees the Proxies’ return to Sixth Street for New Eridu's annual Gilded Carrot Day. At the centre of the celebrations is the debut of idol group Angels of Delusion at the 404 Error music venue, but not all is as it seems.

The story follows the Proxies getting invited backstage to support the group, which also includes helping them set up practice schedules, organise events and manage social media activities. There’s a rhythm minigame as part of that, along with new maps and mechanics for Marcel Adventure.

Angels of Delusion is also the group that the two new Agents being introduced in this update belong to. Members of the same group are capable of performing coordinated attacks. The new arrivals are Sunna and Aria.

Sunna is a an S-Rank Physical Support Agent who specialises in boosting teammates using Attack and Anomaly. Her Ultimate sees her pull out a giant hammer to land heavy damage, and bring teammates into combat using Quick Assist. Sunna’s companion, Bubblegum, can cast Cat's Gaze on enemies, marking them for detonation. Bubblegum can also buff the squad’s attack.

Aria is the other new arrival, the group’s lead vocalist who can shift between two forms, idol projection and construct. Aria is an Ether Anomaly Agent who also deals high burst damage, specifically against enemies who suffer from any Attribute Anomalies.

Sunna and Aria also benefit from the support of the amusingly named Bangboo Biggest Fan, a fan club president who can heal them over time, and boost the squad’s Attack any time two or more Angels of Delusion members are present.

Version 2.6’s S-Rank re-runs are Yixuan (Auric Ink - Rupture), and Yuzuha (Physical - Support), who you can look forward to as part of the banners.

Version 2.6 will also expand Hollow Zero with a new game mode, Operation Matrix. The mode offers themed stages that rotate weekly, each offering new mechanics. You can now also Sweep in Hollow Zero.

Beyond all the celebrations, this update also brings combat kit overhauls to a couple of older S-Rank characters, Lycaon and Harumasa. You can look forward to multiple limited-time events, too, including one where you can earn a new outfit for Pan Yinhu.

The big event is naturally going to be themed around Gilded Carrot Day, and it actually starts today. There’s the usual run of login rewards (about 3,300 Polychromes), as well as daily activities. Yet another login event - Gilded Surprise, Wonderful Boo-ns - will be available February 14-23, offering daily draws from a pool of 4 billion Polychrome.

This extends to mobile and other platforms, with the latest game to grab onto this ongoing craze being Bingo Blitz. But, like any game in this vein, it’s only a matter of time before real money becomes the main option to get credits to keep playing - but in the spirit of staving off that moment and ensuring you need to spend as little of your own money as possible while still enjoying the game, here’s how to get free Bingo Blitz credits for use.

Free Bingo Blitz credits and how to get them The main method is very simple because the developers of Bingo Blitz themselves have clarified that there are no roundabout methods to get them. One important thing to note is that Bingo Blitz warns against potential third-party scammers, so it’s worth taking any sites claiming to offer free credits outside the normal methods with a pinch of salt. #4234. Bandai Namco Shuts Down Unknown 9: Awakening Developer Reflector Entertainment

Bandai Namco has announced it is shutting down Reflector Entertainment, the Montreal studio behind 2024’s Unknown 9: Awakening.

Reflector, founded in 2015, is a subsidiary of Bandai Namco that was acquired in 2020. Unknown 9: Awakening is the studio’s only released title, which was first revealed at Gamescom 2020 and released on October 17, 2024. The third-person action game is set within the broader Unknown 9 transmedia franchise, which includes a book trilogy, comics, and a web series, and stars Haroona, a woman able to traverse a separate dimension called the Fold. Haroona, played by The Witcher actress Anya Chalotra, uses this ability and other supernatural powers to battle a hostile secret society across India and other global locations.

Upon release, Unknown 9: Awakening didn’t make much of a critical splash; it currently has a 59 Metascore and "Mixed" Steam reviews. In November 2024, a month after Unknown 9's launch, Reflector laid off 18 percent of its staff.  More layoffs were announced in January 2025 as Reflector canned an unannounced project while confirming Unknown 9 failed to meet expectations. With Reflector’s dissolution, Bandai Namco expects to post “an extraordinary loss” of approximately €21 million on its Q3 financial results for the fiscal year ending March 31, 2027.

#4233. Starsand Island is a life and farming sim that isn't gacha, and it's out next week

Starsand Island officially has an Early Access release date, and it sounds like it won't stay there for years.

Though it may seem like we just had a big life sim release in Heartopia, 2026 actually has more than one highly-anticipated release in that particular subgenre of cozy game. The next big one on the horizon is Starsand Island, the life and farming sim from Seed Sparkle Lab.

The game has been gaining momentum since the launch of a demo in October last year, but the developer never quite managed to commit to a date for its debut title. Until now.

Seed Sparkle Lab announced today that Starsand Island will enter Early Access on February 11, which is only a bit over one week from now. This goes for Steam and the Xbox Preview Program version.

The developer said to expect a fairly short Early Access run, as the full launch is expected in the summer of this year. When the full release arrives, the game will also make the jump to PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series, as well as Switch 2.

The full release is also expected to bring Steam Deck support and introduce the multiplayer mode, which will not be available during Early Access

Starsand Island has something of a unique look compared to other games in the subgenre. The storybook, anime-inspired aesthetics are popular in the realm of gacha games, of course. However, seeing as this particular game isn’t gacha, being a premium product means it’s going to offer something free-to-play games aren’t designed to.

Speaking of which, the game will be available in two editions: Standard and Deluxe, with the latter including Romanticism-inspired outfits, furniture, and other customisation items. If you buy either during launch, you’ll also get a Chinese New Year bonus with even more outfits and furniture.

On top of the usual systems of farming, mining, and making friends with adorable characters (and animals), the game also has combat that pits you against ancient guardians. You can, of course, also build a home in it, and decorate it to your heart's content.

Seed Sparkle Lab says you can expect about 100 hours of content in the Early Access launch build, and more features will arrive over the course of the next six or so months, including a crossover event with My Time At Portia.

You can look forward to more Starsand Island coverage from us in the near future. Until then, you can get started by planning who you’re going to date now.

#4231. Guide: 50 Best Wii Games Of All Time

19th November 2026 marks the 20th anniversary of Wii's Japanese launch, so it's the perfect time to revisit our list of the best games on the system. Keep an eye out for more Revolution-ary features coming later today and over the weekend!

Nintendo changed the game with Wii, the little motion-controlled console which broke away from the competition and started a revolution. Its brilliantly compact design (the size of three DVD boxes, remember?) and approachable controller helped it open up gaming to a whole new audience, young and old alike.

Despite its reputation as a casual, 'kiddy' console, the huge library of Wii games has some of the most fantastic and varied titles on any system, and the very best Nintendo Wii games took advantage of its unique features in brilliant ways.

To highlight the best of the best, we've compiled the following list of our top 50 Wii games ever.

On this page: 50 Best Wii Games Of All Time

Releasing at the zenith of the plastic instrument craze, Guitar Hero III: Legends of Rock on Wii intergrated the Wii Remote's rumble and speaker into the gameplay — hardly a game changer, but a welcome addition in a game which plays largely the same regardless of platform. Rock on.

One of the very best 3D Sonic games in our books, Sonic Colors managed to translate the classic 2D gameplay and introduce a gimmick that complimented rather than disrupted that gameplay.

The Wisp power-ups gave Sonic new abilities which tied in beautifully to some strong level design and delivered the best Sonic experience we'd ever had in three dimensions. Also available in Ultimate form on Switch.

Bringing two-player cooperative play to the series' chaotic mix of surgery, touch/pointer-based gameplay and drama that makes ER look like a trip to the school nurse, Trauma Center: New Blood made you feel like a regular Dr. Clooney with a Wiimote in your hand instead of a scalpel. It also featured proper character dialogue and diabolical schemes behind the scenes. Let's just hope it's not this dramatic in a real Emergency Room.

And yes, we know the character's name in ER wasn't Dr. Clooney. We know and we don't care.

Pandora’s Tower delivers an involving resource and time-management RPG experience with an imaginative action and combat system. Its overall aesthetic, as well as its focus on a relationship between two characters, are bold design choices that work well as long as you’re willing to invest in the game world.

It’s a pity that the experience, most notably the action segments that take up a large part of the 12-15 hour adventure, are partially undermined by technical failings. As a result, it’s questionable whether many will engage in multiple playthroughs in pursuit of happier endings.

Still, Pandora's Tower has much to recommend it, as long as you’re willing to look beyond some of its faults.

There are plentiful ways to enjoy Cave Story these days, and none of them are bad.

The WiiWare version will be mighty difficult to get hold of if you don't already own it and have it downloaded (the Wii Shop is no longer in operation), but regardless of where or how you play this indie platforming gem, it comes heartily recommended - and this version was a winner.

SEGA found a new home for its light gun games on Wii, and House of the Dead 2 & 3 Return was a must-have title for fans of the series or genre - two classic games fused together perfectly.

Although House of the Dead 2 now feels a little dated, its younger zombie-brother remains excellent, a gore-fest with hours upon hours of zombie-blasting arcade action. Depth and longevity seekers need not apply and should be redirected to a close cousin, Capcom's Resident Evil: The Umbrella Chronicles.

Some might say this is the finest version of the finest Pikmin game, offering the best of all worlds with Wii Remote pointer functionality and a surprisingly good multiplayer component, too.

The sequel might make the fruit look tastier in gorgeous HD, but Pikmin 2 is still the gold standard of the series in our book, whether you play on GameCube, with some New Play Control! on Wii, or on Switch.

A purist might argue that Rock Band 3 suffered from some bloat where its predecessor offered the most streamlined four-man bandplay ever. Each to their own, of course, but when you look at Rock Band 2's playlist and streamlining of the basic experience offered in Harmonix's first entry in the series, the purists might have a point.

Winding back the clock to Mega Man's NES roots with a potent throwback, Inti Creates and Capcom tapped into our nostalgia beautifully with Mega Man 9, returning the bombardier bleu to his original 8-bit stylings in the first numbered entry in the original series for 12 years.

Simply making it look authentic wouldn't have been enough, though. Fortunately, Inti Creates crafted a tight little run-and-gun platformer worthy of bearing that hallowed digit.

An early showcase of the Wii Remote (or the 'Form Baton' as it's known in-game), WarioWare Smooth Moves brought the anarchic micro-gameplay and aesthetic of the handheld series to the Wii in an entry which surely ranks as the most widely played of any WarioWare title.

You never quite knew what was coming next, and this ranks up there alongside Wii Sports as an off-the-wall demonstration of the console's potential in those first few months.

The Wii might not be the first system that springs to mind when asked to think of classic horror games, but Silent Hill: Shattered Memories is up there with the greatest titles in the genre — all the better for really making use of its host console's features, whether it's the speaker in the controller or intelligent use of motion controls to draw you into this reimagining of the Silent Hill series' first entry.

The Making Of Silent Hill: Shattered Memories - Sam Barlow's Wii Masterpiece

Time Extension"I always have to connect things back to the human experience"

There's really only one thing you need to know about Red Steel 2, and that is that the sword combat absolutely, positively delivers in the way you want it to.

The rest of the game does have some issues and without the stellar controls would have been more of a step sideways rather than forward for the genre, but shooting and slicing dudes is just too much fun to pass up.

A foul-mouthed, gorily stylised 'lightgun' shooter in the B-movie mould, The House of the Dead: Overkill has its tongue impaled through its cheek and is best served with buckets of popcorn.

It's yet another slice of mature entertainment on that most family-friendly of consoles, and further proof that the breadth of genres found in Wii's software library was second to none.

World of Goo is a masterful game which marries addictive physics-based puzzling with a fun gooey aesthetic and some biting social commentary to produce one of the best-ever games on Wii or whatever system it appears on.

This special game was a 10 then, it's a 10 now, and shall always remain a 10. And the IR pointer in the original game still trumps the gyro-based equivalent (which needs frequent recentering) and the touchscreen option in the Switch re-release. Just spectacularly good.

Nintendo missed out on any GTAs on its home consoles, but Rockstar's Bully was much more than a consolation prize. Set in the Bullworth Academy, aspiring miscreant Jimmy Hopkins must negotiate the pitfalls and perils of private school life in an open world game that plays a little like a teenage GTA. The Molotov cocktails are replaced with stinkbombs, the AK47s with slingshots.

With an appropriately mischievous and juvenile setting (which arguably suits the sandbox gameplay even better than GTA's mature mayhem), this was a great addition to the 'mature' shelf in the console's library.

There may have been some initial resistance to Visceral’s decision to turn Dead Space into a rail shooter, but the final product is so well-crafted that you can’t help but be impressed by the level of quality it delivers.

Dead Space: Extraction manages to come through on its promise of a cinematic experience by embracing the genre’s limitations and bending the expectations of what an on-rails game can and should do, all the while playing to the Wii’s strengths and pushing its technical abilities to new highs.

While the main story mode may lack in longevity for some, Extraction is definitely worth experiencing at least once, and it’s a title that horror and shooter fans alike shouldn’t miss.

Now available to play on Switch along with its predecessor, No More Heroes 2: Desperate Struggle continues the stylish (mis)adventures of Travis Touchdown in a sequel infused with the same punk-aesthetic, referential humour and sassy surrealism as the first game, except with the splintered edges sanded down to a still-pleasingly rough-and-ready finish.

Another awkward transition to the TV screen for a game which began life on a handheld, we wouldn't recommend playing the WiiWare version of Phoenix Wright: Ace Attorney - Trials & Tribulations these days — besides the fact that you can no longer access the Wii Shop, there are too many excellent alternative ways to play.

This port really should have included pointer controls, but even given its sloppy presentation on Wii, the base game is still pretty ace.

Next Level Games managed to recapture all the character and energy of the original Punch-Out!! on Wii while adding a beautiful cel-shaded graphical style.

With all the fighters from the NES game returning, the motion controls were cute, if a little hit-and-miss, but the option to play using the old-school control style made this a truly excellent update of a classic boxer where it's all about watching your opponent.

An excellent little explorative RTS game that holds its own against the Pikmin series.

You're put in charge of a village and it's your job to ensure your citizens' happiness while expanding your kingdom upwards and outwards. Little King's Story is one of those games that is loved by all who play it, yet remains one of Wii's many 'hidden' gems.

If it sounds at all enticing, we recommend tracking down a copy while they're easy to source — you won't regret it.

A gorgeous side-on action RPG, 2009's Muramasa: The Demon Blade was ahead of the wave of side-scrolling platformers that would arrive from indie studios over the next few years, and Vanillaware's eye-catching adventure through Japanese folklore is still a treat many years later.

Soapbox Vanillaware's Most Underrated Game Is More Than Just A Pretty Picture

PlatinumGames' MadWorld presented an inky black-and-white aesthetic highlighting the ultra-violence of the action whenever red blood sprayed across the screen. Which happened a lot.

Tapping into the visual style of Frank Miller's dark graphic novel Sin City, MadWorld is another example that the Wii's reputation as a family-friendly console, though warranted, is only partially correct. In fact, it had an incredibly varied catalogue and this Sega-published hack-and-slash brawler was a fine example.

Combining the original two Lego Star Wars trilogies from the GameCube era, the now-misleadingly named LEGO Star Wars: The Complete Saga offers hours of low-barrier family fun with dozens of playable characters blasting and lightsaber-ing their way through galactic locales, all to the sound of John Williams' iconic score.

This Danish plastic take on the series was infused with charm from the beginning. Reimagining key scenes from the six movies in silent slapstick (and with DS versions of all of them scaling the games down in a generally admirable fashion), the Lego characters and the comedic, playful tone of the entire game made it a great co-op experience to blast through with friends or younger relatives.

The moveset might be small, but that can't be said for the roster. We can honestly say that leaping around with a Force-infused Yoda (who usually hobbles with a cane) like some crazy, laser-sword-wielding frog is some of the most fun lightsaber combat we've ever engaged in. The fancy-pants newer version on Switch might be better overall, but the original 'complete' Lego Star Wars remains hugely accessible and still brings a smile to our face.

Before the sublime Rayman Legends, there was the sublime Rayman Origins.

A 2D platformer par excellence (as they say in Ubisoft's homeland), the limbless wonder always had an impressive heritage in the platforming genre, but this arguably raised him up alongside the invention and beauty of Nintendo's own offerings — perhaps even higher if you ask players who aren't fans of Super Mario's 'New' adventures.

A Wii port of the 2002 GameCube remake featuring new controls, Resident Evil (or Resident Evil Archives: Resident Evil to give its full title) provides what we came to expect from Wii re-releases of previous-gen titles: a more accessible, incrementally improved control experience with box art that's a bit rubbish.

Just concentrate on the horror of the game rather than the horror of the box and you're golden.

Capcom's adventure Zack & Wiki — a cute pirate/monkey combo — never came to another console, but it's absolutely worth seeking out.

Point-and-click is the name of the game - if you fondly remember Sam and Max or Day of the Tentacle, you will be at home here. You use the Wii Remote to point at the screen and press 'A' to move Zack to that location and check items. When you need to interact with an object, though, you'll need to use gestures (so, to saw down a tree, you need to move the remote forward and backwards repeatedly, etc).

You'd think this would get old fast, but this is a fantastic little adventure and was another great showcase for the hardware back in 2007.

A sequel to Treasure's cult classic N64 rail shooter (which didn't make it to the West until it appeared on Wii's Virtual Console in 2007), this sequel improves on the experience and is arguably the better of the two games — yet another fantastic addition to a huge and impressively varied console library.

We're thankful we didn't have to resort to importing this one back in the day.

A 20th anniversary collection of some of the most popular Kirby games ever, 2012's Kirby's Dream Collection: Special Edition spans the puffball's debut on Game Boy through his NES and SNES adventures and also includes his N64 outing; so, that's Kirby's Dream Land, Kirby's Dream Land 2, Kirby's Adventure, Kirby's Dream Land 3, Kirby Super Star and Kirby 64: The Crystal Shards in one very convenient package.

Convenient for Japanese and North American players, that is — it never saw the light of day in PAL regions. Cue our sad European Kirby eyes.

Super Paper Mario blends classic platformer with some of the RPG elements of its predecessors and throws in a world-flipping mechanic that gives you a whole new perspective on traditional 2D platforming courses. It diverges heavily from Thousand-Year Door's way of doing things, and as a result, divides series fans.

Regardless of where you fall on the spectrum of fandom, the Wii entry is a beautiful game with fiendish puzzles and an intriguing, unique flip mechanic.

A poor port of a great game, we can only assume residual affection for the original software itself is elevating the WiiWare releases in your estimations.

Phoenix Wright: Ace Attorney is a corker, but of the myriad ways available to play it these days, this is probably the last version we'd recommend.

A co-development between Intelligent Systems and Nintendo SPD, Radiant Dawn is a direct sequel to Path of Radiance and could even accept save data brought over from its predecessor which boosted character stats. It was well worth doing, too, as Radiant Dawn was noted for its high difficulty and any advantage was welcome.

This Wii entry brought back dark magic into the fold and increased the scope and number of characters in comparison to Path of Radiance, but wasn't the sales success Nintendo had hoped.

Despite being proclaimed as absolute pinnacles of the series, with many fans citing one of these two as their franchise favourites, the GameCube and Wii entries represented a low point sales-wise, which unfortunately signalled a retreat back to portable hardware only. Indeed, it would be 12 years until the series would grace a television screen once again.

No More Heroes certainly isn’t perfect; the tasks you’re given in between missions are dull (calling to mind the same boredom experienced when you had to get a job in Sega’s Shenmue), the Grant Theft Auto-style driving sections border on pointless (we can only assume they’re intended to be a thinly-veiled dig at the successful franchise), and the general gameplay doesn’t actually change during any of the assassination missions.

But regardless of these points, it still entertains in a way that few other games can manage. It’s a chaotic riot packed with gleeful videogame references, over-the-top dialogue, and some seriously awesome-looking combat action.

A far more accessible proposition than Killer7 ever was, No More Heroes is so wonderfully amusing that it’s easy to forgive its minor shortcomings; Suda 51’s epic fully deserved to garner the kind of attention and praise that unfortunately eluded its predecessor.

The first 2D entry to come to a home console since Mario World in the early '90s, 2009's New Super Mario Bros. Wii brought chaotic — a little too chaotic for some — four-player local multiplayer to the series for the first time.

This game gave old-school fans yearning for a side-on Mushroom Kingdom adventure something to chew on, with plenty of clever nods to the past, although as with the rest of the 'New' series, you could argue that the visual presentation was a little bland. Cracking music in this one, though.

Arriving in a red Wii case which really made it stand out on the shelf, anyone put off by the New series' 'wah's and cuteness missed out on a real platforming treat in NSMB Wii.

Coming from Hironobu Sakaguchi, the creator of Final Fantasy, The Last Story was an impressive RPG and one of the last big releases for the system. While it struggled from a technical perspective at times, it's an ambitious title that's worth playing today if you missed out back in 2012.

Along with Xenoblade Chronicles and Pandora's Tower, it's also notable as one of the titles North American players campaigned to see released in that territory — Nintendo, who published that game elsewhere, eventually granted XSEED publishing rights and it launched six months after PAL regions.

Taking Kirby back to his classic game style following a couple of genre departures, Kirby's Return to Dream Land was a worthy return and yet another glittering gem in the Wii's platforming lineup.

With all the colour and creativity you'd expect from HAL, and a ton of content to delve into, this was a wonderful trip to Kirby's land of dreams.

A gorgeous, low-stress game that transports Kirby into a world of fabric and thread, Kirby's Epic Yarn was the first of Good-Feel's material-based platformers and is arguably still the best.

We adore it. Anyone who says it's lacking in the challenge department is correct... but missing the point entirely. Kirby's Epic Yarn is one of the most joyous and creative games on Wii, or indeed any platform. (It's also available on 3DS in Extra Epic form.)

You played it, your mum played it, your granddad played it; more to the point, you all enjoyed it. Drawing people in with a gimmick is relatively easy, but Wii Sports managed to genuinely entertain entire families and get them playing video games together for an extended period — perhaps for the first time ever.

This pack-in brought huge numbers of people together in silly Mii form and showcased the potential of motion controls to gamers from all generations. It's quite simply one of the most important video games ever made, and the most killer of apps.

Introducing Wii Remote control into Retro's Prime template, Metroid Prime 3: Corruption was an excellent conclusion to the trilogy (well, until the next entry turned up 18 years later to make it a quadrilogy a tetralogy four), a series that proved Samus could not only survive the jump into 3D first-person shooting, but absolutely flourish in that genre.

Originally planned as a Wii launch title, but pushed to August 2007 (a delay? For a Metroid Prime game? Inconceivable!), Prime 3: Corruption as a separate release was subsequently rendered a tad redundant with the launch of the entire trilogy on one glorious disc, but this is still a cracking shooter on its own.

Showcasing the chonky new MotionPlus accessory (eventually built into the updated Wii Remote Plus), Wii Sports Resort offered the kind of motion-tracking fidelity many of us had imagined the Wii would offer out of the gate.

Highlights of this game — which introduced Wuhu Island and expanded on the original game with a bunch of new activities — included fencing and throwing a frisbee for an adorable pooch.

Following the online exploits of Mario Kart DS, it was almost a given that Mario Kart Wii would follow suit and include the ability to play against the world — thankfully, despite the console's rather anaemic online capabilities, the experience was nothing short of stunning.

From the outside, the Wii entry might have sacrificed some of the kart racing series' personality, but the online multiplayer with support for up to twelve players, optional motion controls (who could forget that plastic wheel accessory?), and additional vehicles and characters helped make it one of the most accessible entries in the series.

Successful, too. It sold a staggering 37.38 million copies.

This revival of Rare's treasured Donkey Kong Country series came after developer Retro Studios had successfully reinvented Nintendo's Metroid as an exploratory first-person shooter, so we shouldn't have been surprised that the team was able to recapture the spirit of that 16-bit platformer series three console generations later with Donkey Kong Country Returns. However, just how good the 2010 game turned out still came as a big shock.

The 3DS port was equally impressive, although having played the excellent Tropical Freeze, it's tougher to return (ahem) to Returns these days, even Forever Entertainment's Switch port which combines the two versions into an HD dish with the tiniest dusting of tweaks.

Still, when it comes to resurrections, Retro was Nintendo's go-to studio for a long minute there and DKC swung back in fabulous form on Wii.

The third entry in the scrap-'em-up series, Super Smash Bros. Brawl was the first to introduce Sonic the Hedgehog and Solid Snake, and included the lauded Subspace Emissary mode.

Picking up the baton from the celebrated GameCube entry, Brawl pushed the series in an all-encompassing direction as far as content was concerned, and set the precedent for the 'more is more' approach to stages, fighters, music, and more that kept Masahiro Sakurai occupied eight days a week for many years after.

Showcasing the sort of swordplay we'd hoped Twilight Princess would contain, The Legend of Zelda: Skyward Sword was a beautiful entry in the series which dared to try some new ideas, something the franchise desperately needed at the time.

It arguably didn't get everything right, and why Nintendo ditched the beautifully accurate IR pointer in favour of a gyro alternative which required constant re-centering — especially when everyone already had the IR sensor hooked up anyway! — is still a source of confusion for us. We found the MotionPlus swordplay itself excellent, though.

Chronologically, this is the very first game in the Zelda timeline, so it's pretty much required reading for series fans. While it has its naysayers, we look back on our time with Skyward Sword very fondly.

This was arguably the game which proved that third parties had mastered the grammar of the 3D language Nintendo invented with Ocarina of Time. Okami is a gorgeous Japanese adventure with an oddball cast of characters, fabulous music, and an unforgettable art style.

The HD version on Switch is probably the best way to play these days, but the Wii port of Clover's PS2 original was a delight back in 2008.

A remarkable breath of fresh air for a franchise that was getting a little stale, this put the Resident Evil series on an action-based path away from the fixed-camera, pre-rendered, 'staged' survival horror of the previous games.

What you lost in nail-biting tension was more than made up for by the brilliantly chunky gunplay and impeccable progression through a story that continually ups the ante and adjusts difficulty automatically to keep you on the edge of your seat without pushing you off entirely.

While the additional pointer controls arguably make the Wii version a little too easy, you've still got the option to play with a GameCube controller if you wish (or that chainsaw variant if you're proper hardcore). Subsequent remasters might have upped the resolution, and the remake is a marvel in its own right, but there's a genuine argument that the Wii Edition of Resident Evil 4 remains the best way to play this genre-defining classic, even all these years later.

As groundbreaking as it was, the 3D Zelda formula was starting to look a little tired by the mid-2000s, so while Twilight Princess is a very fine game, it lacked the impact of its predecessors.

The additional 'waggle' implemented in the Wii version didn't live up to the ideas of 1:1 swordplay we'd imagined, either. And did the entire world really need mirroring just to make Link right-handed? Still, at the time this was the only way to play the game in 16:9 and it made for a satisfyingly meaty Wii launch title in North America.

Not one for the purists, perhaps — you'll want to track down an expensive copy of the GameCube version for the left-handed, canonical geography of Hyrule (or just play Twilight Princess HD on Wii U).

2010's Xenoblade Chronicles was epic in scale and setting in a way few games of the era were, and this isn't a title to rush through. You'll need many hours to examine and enjoy its incredible complexity, enhancing your abilities and exploring the world's ecosystem as you go.

The creativity Monolith Soft employed in producing this world was staggering. In terms of presentation, the immense landscapes remain a delight to traverse. While some close-up camera angles expose the Wii's graphical limitations, the art design more than compensates. Although some of the voice acting is hit-and-miss, the soundtrack is superb, genuinely enhancing the experience.

The sublime Definitive Edition on Switch is the easiest and best way to catch up with the first entry these days, but this game delivers a huge (and hugely enjoyable) JRPG experience wherever you play, laying a foundation that Monolith would build on with its sequels.

Collecting the original Prime trilogy in one handy package with new Wii controls for the first two, difficulty options, and other enhancements for the earlier GameCube entries, Metroid Prime Trilogy is arguably one of the best compilation offerings in video games, ever.

The enhanced versions of the first two games were released separately in Japan as part of the New Play Control! line, but in the West we got this thrilling uberdisc.

Purists may point to a handful of missing visual effects compared to the originals, and they're not wrong, but whichever way you look at it, this is a spectacular package - a great way to play these games, and a hardcore crown jewel on the most casual of consoles.

With Super Mario Galaxy 2 Nintendo gave us that rarest of treats — a direct sequel to one of its finest games. While anyone who played and fell in love with Super Mario Galaxy would have been overjoyed to hear there was more on the way, the expectations couldn't have been higher. Somehow, Galaxy 2 expanded on the first game's inventiveness, turning up the colour dial to eleventy-stupid.

This was EAD Tokyo tearing up the textbook and pasting it back together in fascinating, surprising ways, flexing its beefed-up, confidently creative muscles with a huge variety of environments and obstacles, plus Yoshi and a host of new power-ups. It's a brilliant time.

To argue over which Galaxy is better is pointless, really — they're both wonderful and utterly essential, so if you never got around to playing the sequel, carve out some time as soon as possible. Inexplicably, it was missing from the 3D All-Stars collection, but it arrived on Switch eventually. Even if it hadn't, this game is truly worth hunting down a Wii for.

Mini Review Super Mario Galaxy 2 (Switch) - The Stars Align Again In This Cosmic Sequel

Where Sunshine faltered, Super Mario Galaxy truly did shine. Taking Mario into space gave Nintendo the opportunity to play with gravity and give the character a whole new (final) frontier of planetoid playgrounds to blast between, setting the stage for endlessly creative snippets of platforming perfection.

All that aside, there's also Rosalina and the Lumas' story to enjoy if you go looking for it; an affecting and underrated aspect of an utterly sublime game.

It's available to play on Switch (in two flavours, in fact), and you really should — Super Mario Galaxy is an infectiously fun trip through the cosmos which begged the question: Where could the plumber possibly go next?

Mini Review Super Mario Galaxy (Switch) - Still A Stellar Achievement

And there we are — the finest Wii games available to humanity! Such a variety of genres and quality games from all developers, and so many we should catch up on.

Before we finish, let's answer some common questions readers have about the Wii and its catalogue.

The Wii release date was slightly different depending on where in the world you lived, although the three major territories all got it in 2006.

It launched first in North America, followed by Japan a couple of weeks later and the following week in Europe and Australasia.

Here's when Wii released in each of the three main territories:

According to Wikipedia’s list of Wii games, a total of 1612 Nintendo Wii games were released for the console.

The exact number of releases varies depending on the territory (Europe, Japan, North America), but you'll find all Wii games listed by region on that page.

This depends on the model you have. The original Wii is backwards compatible with GameCube games and has controller and memory card ports for its predecessor under the flap on the top side of the console.

Later Wii models — specifically the RVL-101 revision without a stand and the Wii Mini — removed backwards compatibility with GameCube games, unfortunately.

According to Nintendo, Wii Sports is the best-selling Wii game, with 82.90 million copies sold. Wow!

It's worth remembering that Wii Sports has a pack-in with many Wii consoles (and Nintendo sold 101.64 million Wiis in total), so it's unsurprising that it's the most popular Wii game.

In terms of software that was sold separately, the next best-selling Wii game is Mario Kart Wii, which sold 37.38 million copies worldwide. In 2018, a decade after the game launched, we reported the figure as 37.14 million, which means Nintendo managed to shift a further 24,000 copies in the Switch era. Crazy!

You can check out Nintendo's Top 10 if you're interested in the rest of the Wii's best-sellers.

Disagree with this ranking? Do you think Excite Truck or Animal Crossing: City Folk need some love? You can find all Wii games using the search tool below (or via our huge database) and score your favourites out of 10.

Note. In order for games to become eligible, they need a minimum of 50 User Ratings in total for a chance to show up in the ranking.

Feel free to let us know your thoughts on this ranking, as well as your personal Wii highlights, in the comments!

Gavin first wrote for Nintendo Life in 2018 before joining the site full-time the following year, rising through the ranks to become Editor. He can currently be found squashed beneath a Switch backlog the size of Normandy.

#4230. GTA 6: How to Find the Parrot's Secret Stash

Michael Manning (He/Him) has been enamored with video games since he first played the Sonic Classic Collection as a child. With decades of experience in gaming and a full tour as a Gaming Journalist, Michael is ready to step up to the plate. From AAA to the smallest passion projects, his motto is that every piece of ar

Grand Theft Auto 6 is chock full of side quests that point you towards bonus hits or gang hideouts. All over Leonida, groups of ner’do wells are making cash and leaving it lying around, all yours for the taking if you’re quick enough on the draw and know where to look.

GTA 6 is on track to be one of the biggest games of all time, but developers at Rockstar Games still have worries about job security.

While picking up Jason’s neighbor Shirley’s rum order from a nearby liquor store, you just might hear some squawking the attendant writes off as a loud TV. In reality, he’s hiding a pretty penny within an exotic animal ring run out the back, and a spiteful parrot is stuck back there ready to spill the beans. Let’s go over the quickest way to find it and run it for all its worth.

To start, you’ll want to head to the Three Sheers Liquor store, marked on your map by Shirley when you accept her request to snag her rum order. Located just down the road from Jason’s place, enter for a small cutscene hinting there's more going on behind closed doors.

Once you secure Shirley’s rum in your trunk, head down the alley to the right of the store. You’ll hear a bunch of people arguing with what sounds like a parrot, insulting the crew and blabbing about hiding cash. Continue down the alley until you spot an opening in the barbed wire cover on the wall.

Hop over, and the gang will start a brawl. Be careful, as stepping too far away will prompt multiple members to draw their guns. If you want to get out of this quietly and professionally, make sure you handle the group hand-to-hand; that way, no one calls the cops.

Once you handle all the goons, the parrot will start praising you. By interacting with it, Jason will ask about the money it mentioned, and it will start dropping hints. The important one is the generator, alluding to the small box generator in the upper left corner of the yard, behind the liquor store.

Go into focus mode, and you’ll notice a small marked crevice in the side of the store, right beside the generator. Interact with it to pocket a cool $1,382, a solid early-game sum that will more than pay for running Shirley’s errands. You can also pocket a number of melee weapons from the goons, including machetes and shovels if you’re looking for a hand-to-hand option.

The liquor store gang is one of many small, unaffiliated criminal groups that you can find throughout Leonida, acting as a great first taste of the kind of rewards that can be hiding right out of plain sight. Return Shirley’s rum, and you’ve had a very successful errand.
